subject: zoology

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section, SAQ chapter 8 'Locomotion & Reproduction' (book p.41, question 40). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are both STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this card, not merely unrun; 'not checked' must never be read as 'checked and clean'. The mark split is this card's claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. APPEARANCES: the book prints [TS May-19] and [AP M-19,20,22]. BOOK WORDING CORRECTED: the book's point III(1) reads 'Pseudopodium is formed by conversion of gel cytoplasm to sol cytoplasm and vice versa (Sol to gel)', which states the change twice without saying where each one happens. This card gives the standard form: the gel of the ectoplasm turns to sol and flows forward at the advancing tip, and the sol turns back to gel at the sides and rear. The book's own theory names (sol-gel theory, Allen's front contraction or fountain zone theory) and its actin and myosin line are kept. BOOK SPELLING: the book prints 'Lobopodia - Blunt, finger like'; the singular forms lobopodium and filopodium are used here where a single process is meant, matching the book's own VSAQ 129. FIGURE SCOPE: the book prints no pseudopodia figure; this figure is authored from the four type descriptions the book gives, one shape per type, so that the four names are separable by shape and not by memory alone.

steps.why: The word temporary is what makes them false feet: they are formed when the cell moves and withdrawn again, so no permanent limb exists.
common_mistakes: Writing that a pseudopodium is a permanent organelle. It is formed and withdrawn again.
Giving locomotion as the only use. Pseudopodia also collect food.
steps.memory_tip: Pseudo means false and podium means foot: a foot that is made when needed and taken back after.
steps.margin_note: Meaning of the word, then the two uses, then the group. Four short lines.

steps.label: The four types
lines: ray-like, with a stiff axial rod inside.
steps.why: All four names are shape names, so writing the shape beside each name is what earns the mark; the examples are then only a matter of matching one genus to each shape.
common_mistakes: Writing Amoeba as the example for more than one type. Amoeba forms lobopodia only.
Confusing filopodium with reticulopodium. Both are thread-like, but only the reticulopodium forms a network.
steps.memory_tip: Blunt, thread, net, ray: lobo-, filo-, reticulo-, axo-. Four shapes in that order.
steps.margin_note: One line of shape plus one example per type. Do not write paragraphs.

steps.why: The four types are told apart only by shape, so drawing the same cell body four times with a different set of projections is the shortest complete statement of the classification.
common_mistakes: Drawing all four with pointed tips. Only the lobopodium is blunt and rounded.
Drawing the reticulopodium as separate threads. The threads must join into a network.
steps.memory_tip: Same round body four times; change only what comes out of it: blunt lobes, fine threads, a joined net, straight rays.
steps.margin_note: Label each type under its drawing. Four labels, four shapes.

lines.text: Amoeboid movement = sol to gel, gel to sol

steps.why: A pseudopodium is not a new structure but the same cytoplasm changing state, so the explanation is a cycle: stiff to fluid at the front, fluid to stiff at the back.
common_mistakes: Writing that the whole cytoplasm turns to sol. The change happens at the tip and is reversed at the rear.
Naming only one theory. Both the sol-gel theory and Allen's front contraction theory are asked for by the word 'account'.
steps.memory_tip: Gel to sol at the front, sol to gel at the back, and the cell moves forward.
steps.margin_note: End with the two theory names and the cells that show amoeboid movement.

insider_note: The word 'account' means all three parts are wanted — meaning, types with examples, and formation — so a student who writes only the four types rarely gets more than half the marks.
